text: Society guide- lines note there is no general agreement about when prophylaxis should be used. If prophylaxis is to be given to patients with a CD4+ count below 50 cells/microlitre the first drug of choice would be azithromycin; clari- thromycin is an alternative and azithromycin with rifab- utin would be a third choice.3 The UK guidelines, partly based on studies which predate the wide use of HAART, recommend that prophylaxis be continued indefinitely.3 • MYCOBACTERIUM KANSASII INFECTION. UK guidelines state that infections with M. kansasii may be treated with rifampicin (or rifabutin) and etham- butol.3 Pulmonary disease in HIV-negative patients is usually treated for 9 months whereas HIV-positive pa- tients should receive therapy for 2 years or until the spu- tum has been negative for 12 months. For disseminated infection in HIV-positive patients, clarithromycin should be added and possibly also isoniazid. The place of macrolides and fluoroquinolones in pulmonary or disseminated M. kansasii infection remain to be estab- lished. In extrapulmonary disease in HIV-negative pa- tients, chemotherapy with rifampicin and ethambutol may be used before excision of an infected lymph node. In other extrapulmonary disease the guidelines state that the data are insufficient to make recommendations, but consider that rifampicin and ethambutol for 9 months appears sensible with the addition of protionamide and streptomycin and/or a macrolide if the condition is not responding.3 • OTHER OPPORTUNISTIC MYCOBACTERIA. In M. malmoense and M. xenopi pulmonary disease, the UK guidelines recommend that rifampicin and ethambutol should be given for 2 years in HIV-negative patients. Extrapulmonary M. malmoense infections should be treated in the same manner as extrapulmonary MAC or M. kansasii infections. M. malmoense infection rarely occurs in AIDS patients, but if necessary, treat- ment with rifampicin, ethambutol, and clarithromycin, and possibly isoniazid should be used. For M. xenopi in HIV-positive patients the guidelines state that there is no evidence on which to base recommendations; treatment as for pulmonary or disseminated MAC infection is sug- gested.3 For pulmonary disease due to rapidly growing bacteria (M. abcessus, M. chelonae, M. fortuitum, and M. gor- donae) and other species (M. genavense, M. haemophil- um, M. simiae, M. szulgai, and M. ulcerans) surgery should be used if possible.
